source_material: Two groups of trout, each held in four tanks, began a 21-day period at similar mean weights of 90 g and 91 g per fish. Both groups received the same feed twice daily. From day 8, the ration in one group was raised from 1.4% to 1.8% of estimated biomass per day; the comparison group remained at 1.4%. The groups were supplied by separate water lines. Temperature in the increased-ration group fell from 13.4°C to 11.2°C during the period, while the comparison group remained between 13.3°C and 13.5°C. Mean weight gain was 20 g per fish in the increased-ration group and 23 g in the comparison group. Feed delivered averaged 27 g and 25.3 g per fish, respectively; the corresponding feed conversion ratios were 1.35 and 1.10. Uneaten feed was recorded during 6 of 21 observations in the increased-ration group and 1 of 21 in the comparison group. Question: Did increasing the ration improve growth or feed conversion, and can the difference be attributed to ration alone?
outcome_analysis: The increased-ration group gained 20 g per fish compared with 23 g in the comparison group. Its feed conversion ratio was 1.35 compared with 1.10, so the higher ration did not coincide with better performance in these records.
causal_conclusion: The record does not show improved growth or feed conversion after the ration increase: the increased-ration group gained less weight and had a higher feed conversion ratio. The effect of ration cannot be isolated because temperature changed substantially in that group while remaining stable in the comparison group.
causal_uncertainty: The separate water lines make temperature a major alternative explanation for the poorer outcome, and the record does not establish how much feed the fish actually consumed. A comparison with matched temperature conditions and measured feed consumption would be needed to estimate the ration effect more clearly.
confounding_factors: Different temperature trends between the groups, associated with their separate water lines
Tank-level differences in water flow or rearing conditions
Uneaten feed, which means delivered feed may not equal consumed feed
evidence_explanation: The groups started at similar mean weights and received the same feed at the same frequency, while the increased-ration group received more feed. Its lower gain and higher feed conversion ratio argue against an observed performance improvement. However, its water temperature fell while the comparison temperature remained stable, so the outcome difference cannot be assigned to ration alone.
intervention_analysis: The evaluated change was an increase in daily ration from 1.4% to 1.8% of estimated biomass, with feed type and feeding frequency unchanged. More feed was delivered, and uneaten feed was observed more often in that group.
